Ingenuous

/in-JEN-yoo-uhs/ - the stress falls on JEN · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Ingenuous means innocently open, frank, and trusting.

His ingenuous habit of saying exactly what he thought made him a hopeless poker player and a trusted friend.

Worked Example

On her first day in the city, the exchange student was entirely ingenuous: she greeted strangers in the elevator, asked a vendor whether his 'world-famous' pretzels were truly famous, and accepted every answer with delighted belief.

Ingenuous means innocently open and trusting—do not confuse it with ingenious, which means brilliantly clever. An ingenuous question is asked in pure good faith; an ingenious one has a clever design behind it.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

artless: Artless means without performance or design — an artless answer is not arranged to impress anyone. Ingenuous keeps that lack of calculation and adds warmth: the ingenuous speaker is not merely unstudied but openly trusting, offering frank confidences in pure good faith.

trusting: Trusting means ready to believe what other people say — a disposition toward incoming claims. Ingenuous joins that trust to outgoing openness: frank speech, nothing hidden, no angle. A trusting listener believes easily; an ingenuous speaker also lays her own thoughts bare.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

guarded: careful about what is revealed, and to whom

wary: watching for tricks, slow to take things at face value

Where it sits · how far trust outruns worldly judgment — frank → ingenuous → gullible

frank vs. ingenuous: Frank stops short of ingenuous — a frank speaker is simply direct, with worldly judgment intact.

gullible vs. ingenuous: Gullible goes further than ingenuous — open trust has tipped into being easy prey for any trickster.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — in-

Prefix — in-: in, within

Root — genu-

Root — genu-: born (Latin gignere, to be born)

Suffix — -ous

Suffix — -ous: full of

Put it together

Put it together: In- (within) + genu- (born) + -ous = as one was born. Latin ingenuus described the freeborn citizen — and, by extension, the open, honest character a free person could afford to show. English kept that second sense: ingenuous people speak as openly as if they had never learned to hide anything.

Word Choice

formal / warm

Ingenuous praises innocent openness — a child's honesty in an adult conversation. It is one letter away from ingenious ('brilliantly clever'), and the two mean utterly different things: an ingenuous answer is disarmingly honest, an ingenious one is impressively crafty. If the sentence is about cleverness, ingenuous is the wrong word.
